summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Mary Ellen C. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
key_cases.holding: The court of appeals reversed the severance order because the State failed to make reasonable efforts to preserve the family, holding that the duty to provide rehabilitative services with a reasonable possibility of success has a constitutional basis.
key_cases.relevance: Reversal for failure to make reasonable efforts is the principal check protecting the reunification goal.
key_cases.quote: although the State is not obliged to undertake futile rehabilitative measures, it is obliged to undertake those which offer a reasonable possibility of success

key_cases.case_name: Mary Lou C. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
key_cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the severance order, holding that the State's constitutionally grounded obligation to make a reasonable effort to preserve the family applies to the prior-severance ground of A.R.S. § 8-533(B)(10) as it does to other grounds, but affirming because the record supported an implicit finding that further rehabilitative services would have been futile.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the futility exception — the only basis on which the State may dispense with reunification services — against which a failed reunification is measured.
key_cases.quote: The requirement that ADES make an effort to preserve the family is mandated on constitutional grounds

key_cases.case_name: Shawanee S. v. Arizona Department of Economic Security
key_cases.holding: The court of appeals affirmed the termination order, holding that although the agency must prove a diligent effort to provide appropriate reunification services on a length-of-time-in-care ground, a parent who never objects in the juvenile court waives an appellate challenge to that finding.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the service record against which a failed reunification is measured.
key_cases.quote: when ADES seeks severance based on length of time in care, ADES must prove that it "has made a diligent effort to provide appropriate reunification services."

key_cases.case_name: Jessie D. v. Department of Child Safety
key_cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's rights, holding that although the juvenile court misapplied a Michael J. factor, DCS owes incarcerated parents a diligent effort to preserve the family and reasonable evidence supported the best-interests finding.
key_cases.relevance: Diligent agency effort is the precondition to treating reunification as unachievable.
key_cases.quote: DCS must make diligent efforts to preserve the family by providing services to assist parents in maintaining a bond with their children

key_cases.case_name: Brionna J. v. Department of Child Safety
key_cases.holding: The Arizona Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the termination order, holding that the intermediate court misapplied the fifteen-months-in-care ground, reweighed the evidence, used the wrong standard of review, and could not dismiss the dependency in an appeal from the termination order.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the evidentiary frame for deciding when reunification has ceased to be achievable after fifteen months in care.
key_cases.quote: The court of appeals also erred when it exceeded the proper scope of review by reweighing the evidence presented to the juvenile court.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that the 'reasonable efforts' requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), is enforceable by the Secretary through the state-plan approval process but confers no privately enforceable right under § 1983 and creates no implied private cause of action.
key_cases.relevance: Explains why a failed reunification cannot be litigated as a federal statutory violation even where the agency's efforts fell short of the IV-E plan.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that 42 U. S. C. § 671 (a)(15) neither confers an enforceable private right on its beneficiaries nor creates an implied cause of action on their behalf

extended_foster_care_age: Up to age 21 (voluntary extended foster care agreement signed on or after the 18th birthday and before the 21st birthday; the young adult must have been in department custody as a dependent child at age 18, be 18, 19 or 20, and be one or more of: completing secondary education or an educational program leading to an equivalent credential or enrolled in an institution providing postsecondary or vocational education; employed at least 80 hours a month; participating in a program or activity that promotes employment or removes barriers to employment; or unable to be a full-time student or to be employed because of a documented medical condition; A.R.S. § 8-521.02(A))

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met
